summary: Describes the URN namespace identifier for resources published by the Open Mobile Alliance, whose Open Mobile Naming Authority manages them. The document is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It gives the Open Mobile Alliance its own prefix for permanent names, like a dedicated label for its files.

questions: what is the oma urn namespace
how does open mobile alliance identify specifications
how does omna register resource types
subtitle: A namespace for the Open Mobile Alliance to uniquely name mobile specifications and resources.

tldr.problem: The Open Mobile Alliance develops technologies for mobile devices and needs unique, persistent identifiers for the XML descriptions, schemas, and objects those technologies define.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the URN namespace identifier 'oma', which follows the pattern 'urn:oma:{OMAresource}:{ResourceSpecificString}', managed by the Open Mobile Naming Authority (OMNA).
tldr.outcome: OMA-defined objects and specifications can be uniquely identified and referenced, with room for experimental values and delegation to external organizations.

today: RFC 4358 is an Informational RFC that defines the OMA URN namespace for the Open Mobile Alliance. The 'oma' namespace has been registered with IANA and is used by OMA to persistently identify mobile specifications, enablers, and related resources.

sections.title: OMA and the Need for Persistent Names
sections.content:
The Open Mobile Alliance (OMA) is a standards development body that defines technologies for mobile devices. Its membership includes network operators, equipment vendors, content providers, and other suppliers to the mobile market.

As OMA develops 'enablers' (application and service specifications), they need to specify supporting information such as data descriptions, attributes, XML schemas, and object definitions. This information must exist and be available in a unique, reliable, and persistent manner, independent of where it is stored on the internet.

Because OMA's work spans many technical areas and an object could relate to multiple different other namespaces, using a dedicated URN namespace for OMA-defined resources is more practical than binding to multiple external registries. The RFC registers the namespace identifier 'oma' for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: Mobile phone companies create standards for how devices should work. To name all the descriptions and rules they create, they needed their own identifier system that stays the same no matter where the files are stored.

sections.title: The URN Specification
sections.content:
OMA URNs follow this structure:

urn:oma:{OMAresource}:{ResourceSpecificString}

The OMAresource is a US-ASCII string that defines a specific class or type of resource. Examples include 'ac' for Application Characteristic or 'drms' for Digital Rights Management System. Each resource type has its own labeling scheme defined by the ResourceSpecificString, which can also use US-ASCII characters conforming to URN syntax.

The Open Mobile Naming Authority (OMNA) manages the assignment of OMAresource values and the registration of specific strings for each resource class.

Examples of valid OMA URNs include:

  • urn:oma:ac:oma-presence (Application Characteristic for presence)
  • urn:oma:drms:org-foobar (Digital Rights Management System for external organization 'foobar')
sections.plainLanguage: Each name has three parts after 'oma': a category (like 'drms' for Digital Rights), a specific type (like 'org-something'), and identifiers that follow strict rules so names never collide.

sections.title: Authority and Registration Process
sections.content:
The Open Mobile Naming Authority (OMNA) is responsible for managing OMA URNs. OMNA ensures uniqueness of the strings and provides clear documentation of registered uses. The organization publishes registration information on its web site at http://www.openmobilealliance.org/tech/omna.

OMNA manages three types of registration activities:

  • Registered values for OMA specifications and services
  • Registration of values or sub-trees delegated to other external entities
  • Experimental name models for testing purposes (not formally registered)

OMA permits experimental values that are not registered. As a result, multiple users may use the same experimental value for different testing purposes. Since experimental usage is only intended for testing, this is acceptable.

Unique identifiers are ensured by OMNA procedures that prevent duplication, whether the registration is for OMA itself or delegated to external organizations requesting URNs from OMNA.
sections.plainLanguage: One authority (OMNA) manages all the names and keeps a public list of what each one means. They allow special experimental names for testing, as long as they are not mixed up with the permanent, official ones.

sections.title: Persistence and Scope
sections.content:
OMNA maintains registration tables and information in published documentation that covers each OMAresource class separately, with its own description and registration table. This ensures that registered URNs remain persistent and resolvable over time.

The scope of the OMA namespace is global, meaning OMA URNs are valid and resolvable anywhere on the internet. This reflects OMA's international role in mobile standards.

Because OMNA is structured as a separate, long-term authority within OMA, the namespace is expected to persist as long as OMA exists. The registration model is designed so that once a URN is assigned, it is not reassigned to a different resource, ensuring that over time, OMA URNs maintain their value as persistent identifiers.
sections.plainLanguage: Once OMA names something with a URN, that name means the same thing forever. OMA keeps the official list on the internet so anyone can look up what an OMA URN means, anywhere in the world.

references.text: Daigle, L., van Gulik, D., Iannella, R., and P. Faltstrom, "Uniform Resource Names (URN) Namespace Definition Mechanisms", BCP 66, RFC 3406, October 2002.
